Input: Design documents from /specs/001-professional-portfolio-website/

[Story]: Which user story this task belongs to (e.g., US1, US2, US3)

title: Research: Professional Portfolio Website
text:
Feature: Professional Portfolio Website
Phase: 0 - Research & Technology Selection
Date: 2025-10-07


Research Quarto capabilities, best practices for portfolio websites, and resolve any technical unknowns for implementing a professional portfolio site with split-layout hero, project showcase, and blog functionality.





Question: How does Quarto handle multi-page websites with navigation and custom layouts?
Findings: - Quarto uses _quarto.yml for site-wide configuration including navigation menus - Supports website projects with automatic navigation generation - Can define custom layouts using HTML templates and CSS - Built-in support for responsive design and mobile-friendly output - Native support for code syntax highlighting in blog posts
Decision: Use Quarto’s website project type with custom CSS for the minimalist design
Rationale: Quarto is specifically designed for this use case and provides all needed features out of the box without requiring additional frameworks



Question: What’s the best way to organize projects and blog posts in Quarto for easy maintenance?
Findings: - Quarto supports listing pages that automatically aggregate content from directories - Individual .qmd files can include YAML frontmatter for metadata (title, date, tags, description) - Listings can be filtered, sorted, and customized via configuration - Projects and posts can be in separate directories (projects/, posts/)
Decision: Use directory-based organization with YAML frontmatter for metadata
Rationale: Aligns with constitution’s modularity principle - each content item is a separate file with clear metadata
Alternatives Considered: - Single file with all content: Rejected - poor maintainability and violates modularity principle - External CMS: Rejected - adds unnecessary complexity and violates lean architecture principle



Question: How to implement the minimalist split-layout hero design within Quarto’s framework?
Findings: - Quarto allows custom CSS files referenced in _quarto.yml - Can use CSS Grid or Flexbox for split layouts - Quarto generates semantic HTML that can be styled with standard CSS - Can add custom HTML divs in .qmd files using raw HTML blocks
Decision: Custom CSS file (styles/styles.css) with CSS Grid for hero layout
Rationale: CSS-only approach keeps code minimal, maintainable, and within <50 line constraint for any helper functions
Alternatives Considered: - JavaScript framework: Rejected - unnecessary complexity for static content - Quarto theme customization: Rejected - requires understanding Quarto’s Sass variables, CSS more direct



Question: What’s the recommended approach for image optimization in Quarto projects?
Findings: - Quarto doesn’t have built-in image optimization - Manual optimization needed before adding to assets/ - Recommended formats: WebP for photographs, PNG for screenshots with transparency - Standard practice: multiple sizes for responsive images
Decision: Manual pre-optimization of images before adding to repository
Rationale: Simple, one-time process that maintains constitution’s lean approach without build-time complexity
Tools: - ImageMagick or similar for batch conversion/compression - Target: <500KB per image, WebP format preferred



Question: Which static hosting platform works best with Quarto sites?
Findings: - GitHub Pages: Free, built-in GitHub Actions for Quarto - Netlify: Free tier, drag-and-drop or Git integration, better build control - Quarto Pub: Quarto-specific, simplest deployment (quarto publish command)
Decision: Document all three options in quickstart.md, recommend GitHub Pages for Git integration
Rationale: GitHub Pages is free, integrates with existing workflow, and has excellent Quarto support
Alternatives Considered: - Vercel: Good option but GitHub Pages simpler for static Quarto sites - Custom server: Overkill for static content



Question: How to implement the sticky navigation menu that works across all pages?
Findings: - Quarto’s _quarto.yml navbar configuration handles site-wide navigation - Built-in support for sticky headers via theme options - Can customize with CSS for specific positioning/styling needs
Decision: Use Quarto’s built-in navbar with custom CSS for minimal styling
Rationale: Leverages framework features, no custom code needed



Question: How to implement read time estimates, syntax highlighting, and related posts?

## Outcomes: Results, impact, learnings

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with XGBoost
text:
Approach
All work in this project was implemented in Python 3.12.3. Datasets underwent preprocessing and EDA using pandas (v2.2.3). Irrelevant columns and high cardinality features were removed. “Date of Birth” was transformed into “Age.” Columns with >50% missing data were dropped. Ordinal encoding was applied to the column with ordinal data using scikit-learn (v1.6.1) (Pedregosa et al., 2011). Absence counts were binned into categories. One-hot encoding was used for other categorical features. Missing values were addressed by removing observations when the fraction of NAs was below 2%. When needed, feature engineering techniques were applied to create new features that provided additional insights. NumPy (v1.26.4) was used for numerical computations.

Dataset Progression
The original work was performed using a progressive approach, where the dataset was successively enriched to evaluate how additional information impacts model performance:

Stage 1: Core student profiles

After building dozens of analysis pipelines in research and industry settings, I’ve learned that reproducibility must be designed in from the start.

title: Building Reproducible Bioinformatics Pipelines with Python
section: The Five Pillars of Reproducible Pipelines
text:
The Five Pillars of Reproducible Pipelines

1. Environment Management
Never rely on system Python. Always use isolated environments.
# Using conda
conda create -n myanalysis python=3.11
conda activate myanalysis

# Document all dependencies
conda env export > environment.yml
Pro tip: Pin exact versions in production. Use version ranges only during development.


2. Modular Code Structure
Break your analysis into small, testable functions. Each function should do one thing well.
def load_count_matrix(filepath, min_genes=200):
    """Load gene expression matrix and apply basic filtering.
    
    Args:
        filepath: Path to count matrix file
        min_genes: Minimum genes per cell threshold
        
    Returns:
        Filtered AnnData object
    """
    adata = sc.read_csv(filepath)
    sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_genes=min_genes)
    return adata

def calculate_qc_metrics(adata, mt_pattern="^MT-"):
    """Calculate quality control metrics."""
    adata.var['mt'] = adata.var_names.str.startswith(mt_pattern)
    sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(
        adata,
        qc_vars=['mt'],
        inplace=True
    )
    return adata
Notice: - Clear docstrings - Single responsibility per function - Explicit return values - Configurable parameters


3. Configuration Management
Never hardcode parameters. Use configuration files.
# config.yaml
data:
  input_path: "data/raw/counts.csv"
  output_path: "data/processed/"

qc:
  min_genes: 200
  max_genes: 5000
  max_mt_percent: 10

clustering:
  resolution: 0.6
  n_neighbors: 15
# In your pipeline
import yaml

with open('config.yaml') as f:
    config = yaml.safe_load(f)

adata = load_count_matrix(
    config['data']['input_path'],
    min_genes=config['qc']['min_genes']
)
Benefits: - Easy to modify parameters without changing code - Different configs for different experiments - Version control tracks parameter changes


4. Comprehensive Logging
Log everything. Your future self will thank you.
import logging

# Setup logging
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format='%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s',
    handlers=[
        logging.FileHandler('analysis.log'),
        logging.StreamHandler()
    ]
)

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def process_data(adata, config):
    """Process single-cell data with logging."""
    logger.info(f"Starting analysis with {adata.n_obs} cells")
    
    # QC filtering
    n_cells_before = adata.n_obs
    adata = filter_cells(adata, config['qc'])
    n_cells_after = adata.n_obs
    
    logger.info(
        f"QC filtering: removed {n_cells_before - n_cells_after} cells "
        f"({100 * (1 - n_cells_after/n_cells_before):.1f}%)"
    )
    
    return adata


5. Automated Testing (Yes, Even for Analysis Code!)
Test your analysis functions. It catches bugs before they corrupt your results.
import pytest
import numpy as np
import anndata as ad

def test_filter_cells():
    """Test that cell filtering works correctly."""
    # Create test data
    X = np.random.randn(100, 50)
    adata = ad.AnnData(X)
    
    # Add QC metrics
    adata.obs['n_genes'] = np.random.randint(100, 1000, 100)
    
    # Filter
    adata_filtered = filter_cells(adata, min_genes=500)
    
    # Check
    assert all(adata_filtered.obs['n_genes'] >= 500)
    assert adata_filtered.n_obs < adata.n_obs
Run tests with: pytest tests/

text:
A Complete Pipeline Example
Here’s how it all comes together:
# analysis_pipeline.py
import logging
import yaml
import scanpy as sc
from pathlib import Path

# Import your modules
from src.qc import calculate_qc_metrics, filter_cells
from src.normalization import normalize_counts
from src.clustering import find_clusters
from src.visualization import generate_plots

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def run_pipeline(config_path):
    """Run complete scRNA-seq analysis pipeline."""
    
    # Load configuration
    with open(config_path) as f:
        config = yaml.safe_load(f)
    
    logger.info("Starting pipeline")
    
    # Load data
    adata = sc.read_csv(config['data']['input_path'])
    logger.info(f"Loaded {adata.n_obs} cells, {adata.n_vars} genes")
    
    # QC
    adata = calculate_qc_metrics(adata)
    adata = filter_cells(adata, config['qc'])
    logger.info(f"After QC: {adata.n_obs} cells")
    
    # Normalization
    adata = normalize_counts(adata, config['normalization'])
    
    # Clustering
    adata = find_clusters(adata, config['clustering'])
    logger.info(f"Found {adata.obs['cluster'].nunique()} clusters")
    
    # Visualization
    output_dir = Path(config['data']['output_path'])
    output_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    generate_plots(adata, output_dir)
    
    # Save results
    adata.write(output_dir / 'processed_data.h5ad')
    logger.info("Pipeline complete")
    
    return adata

if __name__ == '__main__':
    run_pipeline('config.yaml')

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revolutionized our ability to study cellular heterogeneity and gene expression at unprecedented resolution. However, analyzing scRNA-seq data requires careful attention to data quality, normalization strategies, and biological interpretation.
In this guide, I’ll share best practices learned from analyzing dozens of scRNA-seq datasets in both research and clinical settings.

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Quality Control: The Foundation
Quality control is critical and should never be skipped. Poor quality cells can drive spurious clustering and lead to false biological conclusions.

Key QC Metrics
import scanpy as sc
import pandas as pd

# Calculate QC metrics
sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(
    adata,
    qc_vars=['mt'],
    percent_top=None,
    log1p=False,
    inplace=True
)

# Visualize distributions
sc.pl.violin(
    adata,
    ['n_genes_by_counts', 'total_counts', 'pct_counts_mt'],
    jitter=0.4,
    multi_panel=True
)
What to look for:

Number of genes detected: Typically 500-5000 genes per cell
Total UMI counts: Higher is generally better, but watch for doublets
Mitochondrial percentage: >10% often indicates dying cells

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Normalization: Choosing the Right Method
Normalization corrects for technical variation while preserving biological signal. The choice of method matters.

Standard Approaches

Log-normalization (simple, fast, works for most cases)
SCTransform (variance-stabilizing, good for datasets with high technical noise)
scran pooling (accounts for composition biases)

# In R using Seurat
library(Seurat)

# Log-normalization
seurat_obj <- NormalizeData(seurat_obj, normalization.method = "LogNormalize")

# Or SCTransform for variance stabilization
seurat_obj <- SCTransform(seurat_obj, verbose = FALSE)
My recommendation: Start with log-normalization. Only move to SCTransform if you see batch effects or high technical noise.

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Clustering: Finding Cell Populations
Clustering identifies groups of cells with similar expression profiles. But remember: clusters are computational artifacts - biological validation is essential.

Best Practices

Test multiple resolutions: Don’t settle on the first clustering result
Use biological markers: Validate clusters with known cell type markers
Check for over-clustering: Are “different” clusters really distinct?

# Leiden clustering at multiple resolutions
for res in [0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0]:
    sc.tl.leiden(adata, resolution=res, key_added=f'leiden_{res}')
    
# Visualize
sc.pl.umap(adata, color=['leiden_0.6', 'CD3E', 'CD14'], ncols=3)

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Differential Expression: Statistical Rigor Matters
Finding marker genes requires appropriate statistical methods. Avoid these common pitfalls:

Don’t use t-tests on log-normalized data (violates assumptions)
Correct for multiple testing (use Benjamini-Hochberg FDR)
Report effect sizes, not just p-values

# Wilcoxon rank-sum test (robust, non-parametric)
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(
    adata,
    groupby='leiden',
    method='wilcoxon',
    use_raw=True
)

# Filter by log-fold change and adjusted p-value
sc.tl.filter_rank_genes_groups(
    adata,
    min_fold_change=1.5,
    max_pval_adj=0.05
)

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Biological Interpretation: The Real Challenge
This is where domain expertise becomes critical. Computational analysis tells you what changed, but only biology tells you why it matters.

My Workflow

Annotate clusters using established markers
Validate surprising findings with orthogonal methods (IF, flow cytometry)
Place results in biological context - what does this mean for the system?
Share findings with collaborators early and often

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Common Pitfalls to Avoid
❌ Batch effects: Always check for batch-driven clustering
❌ Doublets: Remove them early or they’ll dominate analysis
❌ Over-interpretation: Not every cluster is a novel cell type
❌ Ignoring biology: Computational results need biological validation

title: Best Practices for Single-Cell RNA-Seq Data Analysis
text:
Conclusion
scRNA-seq analysis is powerful but requires careful methodology. Focus on quality control, choose appropriate statistical methods, and always validate computationally-derived conclusions with biological experiments.
The key is balancing computational rigor with biological insight - neither alone is sufficient.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Problem
Educational institutions face challenges in identifying at-risk students early enough to intervene effectively. Traditional methods often rely on reactive indicators rather than predictive analytics. Understanding which factors most strongly predict dropout risk—and at what stage of a student’s journey—is crucial for developing effective retention programs.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Approach
All work in this project was implemented in Python 3.12.3. Datasets underwent preprocessing using pandas (v2.2.3). Irrelevant columns and high cardinality features were removed. “Date of Birth” was transformed into “Age.” Columns with >50% missing data were dropped. Ordinal encoding was applied to “CourseLevel” using scikit-learn (v1.6.1) (Pedregosa et al., 2011). Absence counts were binned into categories. One-hot encoding was used for other categorical features. Missing values were addressed by removing observations when the fraction of NAs was above 2%. For Stage 3, “RateModuleSuccess” was computed. NumPy (v1.26.4) was used for numerical computations.

Dataset Progression
We developed a dropout prediction system using three progressive datasets:

Stage 1: Core student profiles (demographics, course information)
Stage 2: Engagement metrics (authorized/unauthorized absences)

Stage 3: Academic performance (module pass/fail rates)



Methodology

Preprocessing: Data encoding, scaling, and feature engineering
Models: XGBoost and Neural Networks with hyperparameter tuning
Evaluation: ROC-AUC, F1-score, precision-recall metrics
Comparison: Performance analysis across all three data stages

title: Feature Specification: Professional Portfolio Website

Created: 2025-10-07
Status: Draft
Input: User description: “Professional Portfolio Website with Quarto”




A visitor lands on the portfolio website to learn about the professional’s background, expertise, and current work. They need to quickly understand who this person is, what they do, and how to contact them.
Why this priority: This is the primary purpose of the portfolio - establishing professional identity. Without this, the site fails its core mission. Every visitor needs this information regardless of what else they’re looking for.
Independent Test: Can be fully tested by navigating to the home page and verifying that profile information, contact methods, and professional summary are all visible and accessible within the hero and about sections.
Acceptance Scenarios:

Given a visitor lands on the home page, When they view the hero section, Then they see the professional’s name, title, tagline, a call-to-action button, and professional photograph
Given a visitor scrolls to the about section, When they read the content, Then they find a 2-3 paragraph bio covering professional identity, expertise areas, and current work
Given a visitor wants to make contact, When they look for contact options, Then they find working links to email, LinkedIn, and GitHub
Given a visitor wants more details, When they look for additional information, Then they find a downloadable resume/CV link





A potential employer or collaborator wants to see concrete examples of the professional’s work to evaluate their capabilities and experience. They need to browse projects, understand what was built, and assess the quality of work.
Why this priority: Showcasing work is the second most important function - it provides evidence of claims made in the profile. This is what differentiates a portfolio from a simple bio page.
Independent Test: Can be fully tested by navigating to the projects page, viewing project cards, clicking into individual projects, and verifying all project details are displayed correctly with working links.
Acceptance Scenarios:

Given a visitor clicks “View Projects” from the home page, When the projects page loads, Then they see a grid of project cards displaying thumbnails, titles, brief descriptions, technology tags, and completion dates
Given a visitor browses the featured project on the home page, When they view it, Then they see a large project image, title, description, technology tags, and links to view the full project or all projects
Given a visitor clicks on a project card, When the individual project page loads, Then they see the project title, hero image, full description including problem/solution/technologies/outcomes, visual content, and links to GitHub repo or live demo
Given a visitor views a project, When they want to return, Then they can use the “Back to Projects” navigation
Given a visitor wants to explore by technology, When filtering options are available, Then they can filter projects by technology or category





A professional peer or someone interested in the professional’s expertise wants to read technical blog posts to understand their thinking, learn from their experiences, or assess their knowledge depth.
Why this priority: Blog content demonstrates thought leadership and expertise but is not essential for the initial portfolio launch. A site can function without blog posts initially, making this lower priority than profile and projects.
Independent Test: Can be fully tested by navigating to the blog page, viewing post previews, clicking into individual posts, and verifying all content is readable with proper formatting and navigation.
Acceptance Scenarios:

Given a visitor navigates to the blog page, When the page loads, Then they see a chronological list (newest first) of blog post previews with title, date, excerpt, read time, and “Read More” link
Given a visitor clicks on a blog post preview, When the individual post page loads, Then they see the full post with title, publication date, formatted content, code syntax highlighting (if applicable), author info, and “Back to Blog” navigation
Given a visitor wants to find specific topics, When categories/tags are available, Then they can filter posts by category or tag
Given a visitor reads a post, When they finish, Then they see suggestions for related posts

What happens when images fail to load? (Display alt text and placeholder)
What happens when a visitor uses a very small mobile screen? (Content stacks vertically, maintains readability)
What happens when someone tries to access a non-existent project or blog post? (Display friendly 404 with navigation back to main sections)
What happens when the resume/CV file is not available? (Hide the download link or show “Coming Soon”)
What happens when there are no blog posts yet? (Display message: “Blog posts coming soon” with option to view projects)

The site prioritizes simplicity, performance, and accessibility over complex features. The modular structure (separate files for projects and blog posts) allows for easy content additions and updates over time.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with XGBoost
text:
Hyperparameter Tuning with GridSearchCV

# Grid Search for Hyperparameter Tuning

param_grid = {
    'learning_rate': [0.01, 0.05, 0.1],      # Lower for better generalization
    'max_depth': [4, 6, 8],                   # Control tree complexity
    'min_child_weight': [1, 3, 5],            # Prevent overfitting
    'gamma': [0, 0.1, 0.2],                   # Regularization
    'subsample': [0.6, 0.8, 1.0],             # Stochastic sampling
    'colsample_bytree': [0.6, 0.8, 1.0],      # Feature sampling
    'n_estimators': [50, 100, 150]            # Number of trees
}

grid_search = GridSearchCV(
    estimator=xgb.XGBClassifier(
        eval_metric='logloss',
        early_stopping_rounds=10,
        random_state=42
    ),
    param_grid=param_grid,
    scoring='roc_auc',  # Optimize for AUC
    cv=3,               # 3-fold cross-validation
    n_jobs=-1           # Use all CPU cores
)

grid_search.fit(X_train_s3, y_train_s3, eval_set=[(X_val_s3, y_val_s3)], verbose=False)
best_params_s3 = grid_search.best_params_

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with XGBoost
text:
Initialise model with best parameters

# Initialize model with optimized hyperparameters
xg_model_best_param_s3 = xgb.XGBClassifier(
    random_state=42,
    n_estimators=100,           # Number of boosting rounds
    max_depth=6,                # Tree depth
    learning_rate=0.1,          # Shrinkage factor
    subsample=0.8,              # % of samples per tree
    colsample_bytree=0.6,       # % of features per tree
    eval_metric='logloss',      # Metric for early stopping
    early_stopping_rounds=10,   # Stop if no improvement
    min_child_weight=1,        # Prevent overfitting
    gamma=0.1                  # Regularization
)

# Train with validation monitoring
xg_model_best_param_s3.fit(
    X_train_s3, y_train_s3,
    eval_set=[(X_val_s3, y_val_s3)],  # Early stopping data
    verbose=False                # Show training progress
)

# Predictions
predictions_best_param_s3 = xg_model_best_param_s3.predict(X_val_s3)

# Evaluation
print("Validation Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_val_s3, predictions_best_param_s3))
print("\nClassification Report (Best Parameters):")
print(classification_report(y_val_s3, predictions_best_param_s3))

# Confusion Matrix
cm_best_param_s3 = confusion_matrix(y_val_s3, predictions_best_param_s3)
cfmd_best_param_s3 = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm_best_param_s3, display_labels=["no","yes"])
# Create plot and remove grid lines
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cfmd_best_param_s3.plot(ax=ax, colorbar=False)
ax.grid(False)  # This removes the white crossing lines
# Make numbers more visible
for text in ax.texts:
    text.set_size(14)  # Larger font size
    text.set_color('lightblue')  # Force black text
plt.show()

# Feature Importance
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plot_importance(xg_model_best_param_s3, max_num_features=20)  # Top 20 features
plt.title('Feature Importance')
plt.show()

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with XGBoost
text:
Testing model on testing data

# Calculate ROC curve
y_pred_proba_best_param_s3 = xg_model_best_param_s3.predict_proba(X_test_s3)[:, 1]  # Probabilities for AUC using test set
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_test_s3, y_pred_proba_best_param_s3) # Use TEST set for final evaluation
roc_auc_best_param_s3 = auc(fpr, tpr)

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.plot(fpr, tpr, color='darkorange', lw=2, 
         label=f'ROC curve (AUC = {roc_auc_best_param_s3:.4f})')
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color='navy', lw=2, linestyle='--', label='Random Guess')
plt.xlim([0.0, 1.0])
plt.ylim([0.0, 1.05])
plt.xlabel('False Positive Rate (FPR)', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('True Positive Rate (TPR)', fontsize=12)
plt.title('ROC Curve Tuned Stage 3', fontsize=14)
plt.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

Evaluation Framework: Models used 80:20 stratified train-test splits with StandardScaler normalization. Metrics included ROC-AUC, precision, recall, and F1-score (weighted average). Class-specific metrics addressed imbalance. Confusion matrices and SHAP values enhanced interpretability. ROC-AUC on validation sets selected the best model. Class imbalance was addressed by focusing on precision-recall tradeoffs for minority classes.
The transition from Stage 1 to Stage 2 significantly improved model performance, driven by the inclusion of student absence data (See Notebook). This data enabled XGBoost to enhance accuracy and discrimination, particularly for at-risk students (minority class 0). The base XGBoost model’s ROC AUC increased from 0.85 (Stage 1) to 0.89 (Stage 2), with engineered features like Unauthorised_Absence_Ordinal and Autorised_Absence_Ordinal improving minority class recall. A tuned Stage 2 XGBoost model achieved a 0.89 ROC AUC on the testing dataset, a notable improvement from Stage 1’s 0.86 (See table 1).
Stage 3’s introduction of RateModuleSuccess further enhanced prediction, with base XGBoost models reaching a 0.993 ROC AUC on the testing dataset. Interestingly, hyperparameter tuning at this stage yielded minimal improvements, achieving a 0.994 ROC AUC (See table 1). XGBoost models showed significant improvement across stages, particularly in detecting at-risk students. The inclusion of absence data and RateModuleSuccess had a greater impact on model performance than tuning, indicating these features were primary drivers of enhancement.
